nameStory: The name "Jagged Notchwort" comes from the deeply cut, notched leaves that look like they've been snipped with tiny scissors. The word "notchwort" is an old botanical term for plants with indented or notched foliage, while "jagged" describes the irregular, zigzag pattern of these cuts.
description: Jagged Notchwort is a tiny leafy liverwort that forms small, delicate patches on rocks and soil. This diminutive plant grows as flat, creeping mats rarely more than an inch across, with overlapping leaves arranged in two rows along thread-like stems. Each leaf is deeply divided into narrow, pointed segments that give the plant its characteristic jagged appearance. Like all liverworts, it lacks true roots, flowers, or seeds, instead reproducing through spores.

idTips.label: Deeply notched leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are split almost to the base into 3-5 narrow, pointed lobes that feel papery-thin between your fingers

idTips.label: Two-ranked arrangement
idTips.description: Leaves attach to the stem in two neat rows, creating a flattened, ladder-like appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Creeping growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms small, spreading mats that feel slightly spongy and springy when gently pressed

idTips.label: Brownish-green color
idTips.description: Usually dull brownish-green to olive, sometimes with reddish tinges at the leaf tips, never bright emerald green

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual plants are typically less than half an inch long, requiring close inspection or a hand lens to see details clearly

habitat: **Note: Information about habitat is uncertain due to limited data** This rare liverwort likely grows on moist, shaded rocks, soil banks, and rotting logs in cool, humid forests. Based on related species, it probably prefers acidic substrates in areas with consistent moisture, such as stream banks or north-facing slopes at higher elevations.

seasonality.spring: Most visible as winter moisture supports active growth. Look for the characteristic jagged leaf pattern emerging from winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: May become less conspicuous during dry periods, with leaves appearing more brownish and contracted. Still identifiable by leaf shape if substrate remains moist.
seasonality.fall: Often shows renewed growth with fall rains. This is an excellent time to spot the distinctive notched leaves as other vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Persists through winter in protected locations, appearing darkened but maintaining its jagged leaf structure under snow or leaf litter.

funFact: **Uncertain claim** This tiny plant can allegedly survive being completely dried out for months, then spring back to life within hours when water returns - a superpower that makes it one of nature's most resilient resurrection plants!
confusionNotes: **Uncertain identification notes** Most likely confused with other small leafy liverworts, but the deeply jagged, multi-lobed leaves are distinctive. Remember: if the leaves look like tiny green hands with many pointed fingers, you've likely found Jagged Notchwort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name ending in "-wort" (an old English word meaning plant), this isn't related to flowering plants at all. Liverworts are actually more closely related to mosses and represent some of the earliest land plants on Earth, making them living fossils in your backyard.
compareHints: **Uncertain comparison** Since this is the only Schistochilopsis species in New England, compare it to other members of the Scapaniaceae family by looking for the deeply divided leaves - most related liverworts have simpler, less dramatically notched foliage. The multiple narrow leaf lobes set Jagged Notchwort apart from its cousins.
